opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: Thanks for making time, Mick. I'm a researcher with the Work Futures Panel, an independent group that studies how people see changes at work, and nothing you tell me will be linked to your name.

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: No worries. Fair warning, I'm more of a hammer and tape measure man than a computer man.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Picture this. AI stays a handy tool, like a better search engine. Hiring, pay and prices carry on the way they would have anyway. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say it's handy for quotes and emails. My bookkeeper uses it to tidy things up. It doesn't build houses.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Nothing changes. My real problem is the one I've had for ten years. I can't find enough good tradespeople who turn up.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do in the first year? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Same as always. Chase subcontractors, chase permits, chase payments. Try again to hire a decent apprentice.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Fine. Busy, but fine.

S0.say: It's handy for quotes and emails. It doesn't build houses.
S0.think: Nothing changes. My real problem is still finding tradespeople who turn up.
S0.do: Chases subcontractors, permits and payments as usual, and tries again to hire a decent apprentice.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Now picture this. Very capable AI exists, but it spreads slowly, over ten years or more. Some tasks disappear, but few whole jobs do. Companies hire fewer beginners. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say slow is sensible. And if companies are hiring fewer beginners, send them to the trades. We're crying out for them.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Fewer office starters might push young people my way. That'd be a win. I'd take two more apprentices tomorrow if they'd turn up.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do in the first year? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Talk to the local school about apprentices. Maybe try the AI thing for my quotes and scheduling.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Pretty good, actually. Hopeful.

S1.say: If companies hire fewer beginners, send them to the trades. We're crying out for them.
S1.think: Fewer office starters might push young people my way. That'd be a win.
S1.do: Talks to the local school about apprentices and tries AI for quotes and scheduling.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Next one. Within 5 years, AI assistants that can act on their own handle most routine office work. There are layoffs and pay pressure in office jobs. Some new AI-related jobs appear, and politicians argue loudly about what to do. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say learn a trade. Nobody's sending an AI to fix your roof. And the government should get out of the way instead of handing out money.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Probably good for me. Some office people who lose their jobs will want to work with their hands. Only worry is if people stop buying houses.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do in the first year? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Put an ad out for career changers and offer them some training. Keep the books careful in case sales slow.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Fine. A bit watchful about the housing market.

S2.say: Learn a trade. Nobody's sending an AI to fix your roof.
S2.think: Probably good for me. Office people will want to work with their hands. The worry is if people stop buying houses.
S2.do: Advertises for career changers with some training on offer, and keeps the books careful.
S2.feel: Fine, watchful about the housing market.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Now a faster version. Within 2 to 3 years, AI matches skilled professionals at most thinking work. Lots of office and professional workers lose their jobs. Share and house prices boom. There's a political crisis over who should get the gains. Physical jobs are mostly untouched. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say this proves what tradespeople have known for years. Real work matters. And keep the government's hands off people's money.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: House prices booming means people want to build and renovate, which is good for me. But if lots of office people are out of work, who's buying? The ones who did well, I suppose. I'd chase the top end.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do in the first year? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Go after bigger renovations for people doing well out of the boom. Take on the career changers. Put a bit more away.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Mostly good. Keeping an eye on who's left to buy.

S3.say: This proves what tradespeople have always known. Real work matters.
S3.think: The boom means people want to build. The question is who's left to buy, so I'd chase the top end.
S3.do: Goes after bigger renovations for people doing well in the boom, takes on career changers and saves a bit more.
S3.feel: Mostly good, eye on who's left to buy.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Last one. Everything in the previous picture happens, and on top of that, general-purpose robots arrive in warehouses, kitchens, building sites, farms and care homes within 3 to 5 years. Hands-on work is no longer a safe place to be. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say if a robot turns up on time and doesn't call in sick on a Monday, I'll hire it. And I'd mean it.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: But the big developers will buy robots first, by the dozen. They'll build cheaper and faster than a small outfit like mine. My eight blokes are like family. I don't know how I'd compete, and I'm not about to run a robot crew from an app.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do in the first year? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Go and see one working before I believe a word of it. Then ask the bank about leasing one rather than buying. Focus on the work robots can't do well yet, like old houses and awkward renovations.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Anxious. Wanted the help, didn't want the competition.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You've said you'd welcome a robot that shows up on time. Do you still?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: On my site, yeah. On the big boys' sites, that's what worries me.

S4.say: If a robot turns up on time and doesn't call in sick, I'll hire it.
S4.think: The big developers buy them by the dozen and build cheaper than me. I don't know how my eight blokes and I compete.
S4.do: Goes to see a robot working, asks the bank about leasing one, and focuses on old houses and awkward renovations.
S4.feel: Wanted the help, didn't want the competition.
